Goal: skip parsing, indexing and storage for pages we already hold
**Exact**: store ==SHA-256== of the body in a KV store

**Near**: ==SimHash== gives a **64-bit** fingerprint per page
Near-dupes if ==Hamming distance ≤ 3== (at most 3 differing bits)
Scanning every fingerprint for distance ≤ 3 is too slow
Split the 64-bit SimHash into ==4 blocks of 16 bits==, index each block
Distance ≤ 3 flips at most 3 bits, so at least **1 block** is identical
Fetch candidates sharing a block, then verify the full Hamming distance

blocks.q: A crawler runs 10 workers that all pop from one shared queue. Host X has 500 URLs queued next to each other. What goes wrong, and what is the fix?
a_bullets: Several workers pop X's URLs at the same moment, so X gets parallel requests and the 1 request/sec rule is broken.
X may rate-limit with 429s or block the crawler.
Fix: route each URL to a back queue by `hash(host)`, so one host lives in one queue.
Give each back queue to a single worker, and use a heap keyed by next-allowed-time to pick the next host.

blocks.q: The seen-URL check uses a Bloom filter: 'seen' means skip, 'not seen' means enqueue. Which mistake can it make, and which can it never make?
a_bullets: It can say 'seen' for a URL that is actually new (false positive), so that URL is silently never crawled.
It can never say 'not seen' for a URL it has stored (no false negatives), so a miss means definitely new.
At 1% false positives it needs about 9.6 bits per URL, so 10B URLs take about 12 GB.
An exact 64-bit hash set takes 80 GB, roughly 7x more. Use the Bloom filter first and go to the KV store only on a hit.

blocks.q: Spot the bug: the pipeline hashes each extracted link for the seen-URL check, then normalizes it. Page links include `http://A.com/page` and `http://a.com:80/page#top`. What happens?
a_bullets: The raw strings differ in host case, port and fragment, so they hash differently.
Both count as new and both are enqueued, so the same page is fetched twice.
Fix: normalize first (lowercase host, drop the default port, strip the fragment, sort query params).
Both links then become `http://a.com/page`, and the second one is caught as already seen.

blocks.q: Peak load is 1,200 fetches/sec and each fetch takes about 500 ms. A node holds 60 connections. How many nodes do you need? What if average latency doubles to 1 s?
a_bullets: Concurrent connections = rate x latency = 1,200 x 0.5 s = 600.
600 / 60 per node = 10 nodes.
At 1 s latency you need 1,200 connections, so 20 nodes. Latency matters as much as request rate.
Slow hosts are the usual cause, so per-fetch timeouts (connect 5 s, read 30 s) also protect capacity.

blocks.q: Two pages have 64-bit SimHash values that differ in exactly 3 bits. Are they near-duplicates? Why does indexing four 16-bit blocks still find them?
a_bullets: Yes. The rule is Hamming distance ≤ 3, and 3 qualifies.
3 differing bits can touch at most 3 of the 4 blocks, by the pigeonhole principle.
So at least one 16-bit block is identical in both fingerprints.
A lookup on each block's index returns candidates, and a full 64-bit Hamming check then confirms or rejects each one.
